title: Horner Syndrome: The Oculosympathetic Roadmap

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Horner Syndrome (oculosympathetic paresis) results from an interruption of the sympathetic nerve supply to the eye and adnexa. It is classically defined by the triad of miosis, ptosis, and anhidrosis. While often benign, its sudden onset—especially when accompanied by pain—can signal life-threatening conditions such as internal carotid artery dissection (ICAD) or Pancoast tumor.

sections.title: The Three-Order Neuron Pathway
content: 1st Order (Central): Hypothalamus → Ciliospinal Center of Budge (C8-T2). Passes through the brainstem.
2nd Order (Pre-ganglionic): Ciliospinal Center → Over the Lung Apex → Superior Cervical Ganglion (Level of Mandible/C2).
3rd Order (Post-ganglionic): Superior Cervical Ganglion → Carotid Plexus → Through Cavernous Sinus → Long Ciliary Nerves → Iris Dilator & Müller's Muscle.

rows: Pancoast Tumor (Lung), Thoracic Aneurysm, Birth Trauma (Klumpke), Iatrogenic (Surgery)
Arm pain, hand muscle wasting (T1 involvement)
Carotid Dissection, Cluster Headache, Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis, Raeder Syndrome

sections.title: The Painful Horner: RED ALERTS
content: Internal Carotid Artery Dissection (ICAD) until proven otherwise.
Acute onset of facial, neck, or periorbital pain.
Amaurosis Fugax or TIA-like symptoms.
History of minor neck trauma (e.g., yoga, chiropractic, coughing).
Associated CN XII palsy (suggests extracranial CAD).

sections.title: Clinical Signs & Ocular Findings
content: Miosis: Anisocoria is greater in the dark (dilation lag).
Ptosis: Mild (1-2mm) due to Müller's muscle weakness.
Upside-down Ptosis: Elevation of the lower eyelid.
Anhidrosis: Loss of sweating (Total face: 1st order; Forehead only: 3rd order).
Iris Heterochromia: If congenital (affected eye is lighter).
Apparent Enophthalmos: Due to narrow palpebral fissure.

sections.title: Pharmacological Testing Protocol
content: Step 1: Apraclonidine 0.5% or 1% (Diagnosis). Horner pupil dilates; normal pupil does not (reversal of anisocoria).
Step 2: Cocaine 4% or 10% (Gold Standard Diagnosis). Horner pupil fails to dilate; normal pupil dilates.
Step 3: Hydroxyamphetamine 1% (Localization). Dilates 1st/2nd order; fails to dilate 3rd order.
Step 4: Phenylephrine 1% (3rd order check). Significant dilation suggests 3rd order due to denervation supersensitivity.

branches: Dark > Light (Sympathetic): Horner, Physiological Anisocoria, Long-standing Argyll Robertson
Light > Dark (Parasympathetic): Adie Tonic Pupil, CN III Palsy, Pharmacological Mydriasis, Trauma/Sphincter Damage

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Strategy
content: 1. Confirm Diagnosis (Apraclonidine/Cocaine test).
2. Determine Urgency: If PAINFUL → Immediate ER referral for MRA Head/Neck.
3. Localize: Check for associated CN palsies or 'long-tract' signs.
4. Imaging: MRI Brain, MRA/CTA Head & Neck, CT/X-ray Chest (Apex).

content.explanation: Ptosis, Anhidrosis, and Miosis = Horner Syndrome.

sections.title: Imaging Specifics for CAD
content: Axial T1 with FAT SATURATION is the gold standard for detecting intramural hematoma.
MRA or CTA of the neck must include the 'carotid string sign'.
Scan from the Arch of the Aorta to the Circle of Willis.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
content: Most common cause: Birth trauma (brachial plexus injury).
Crucial Red Flag: Neuroblastoma (must check urinary catecholamines/VMA).
Characteristic Sign: Iris heterochromia (hypochromia on the affected side).

sections.title: Surgical Management
content: Müller Muscle Conjunctival Resection (MMCR): For correcting the mild ptosis.
Fasanella-Servat Procedure: A variation of MMCR often used.
Levator Aponeurosis Advancement: Reserved for larger ptosis components.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls (High Yield)
content: Dilation Lag: The anisocoria is most prominent 5 seconds after lights out.
Wallenberg Syndrome: Expect ipsilateral Horner + contralateral loss of pain/temp.
Apraclonidine False Negative: May occur in very acute cases (<48 hours) due to lack of receptor upregulation.

sections.title: Landmark Studies: The 'Pain' Evidence
sections.content: A landmark study by Biousse et al. noted that Horner syndrome occurs in approximately 25% to 58% of internal carotid artery dissections. In many cases, it is the *only* presenting sign before a major stroke occurs. Immediate anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy is often required once the dissection is confirmed by imaging.

sections.title: Summary of Complications
content: Ischemic Stroke (if CAD is missed).
Metastatic spread of occult malignancy (Pancoast tumor).
Permanent ocular cosmetic defects (ptosis).
Progression of underlying neurological disease (MS/Tumor).
